articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. There were stiff boxy pleated skirts and tube skirts painted with swirls, and dainty embellished skirts with a layer of gauze on top, like a petticoat worn on the outside. Continue reading...

articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a lab coat and examine brain regions and neurochemicals, but studying the mechanics, he says, doesn’t damp down the mysteries of consciousness. “For me, actually, I’ve become more spiritual and interested in the world of mystery and, I want to say supernatural, but dimensions that are intangible, by studying something like sleep paralysis.” Continue reading...

articles.title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
articles.description: We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary Birds of War , which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC , and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence. The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions. “Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.” Birds of War premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

articles.title: Meet David Morales: Providence Voters Elect Democratic Socialist Mayor, Approve Israel Divestment
articles.description: Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence. “What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. And for that reason, we are seeing a rise in democratic socialism and the representation of democratic socialists all across the country.”

articles.title: "American Scoundrel": From Roy Cohn to Stephen Miller, "McCarthyism Lives On," Says Author Kai Bird
articles.description: We speak with historian Kai Bird about American Scoundrel , a new biography of the notorious political fixer Roy Cohn, who rose to fame as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy during the senator’s anti-communist campaign, served as a lawyer for the New York mob, and was an influential voice in Republican circles until his death from AIDS -related complications in 1986. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s. Facing political setbacks during his first term as president, Trump reportedly asked, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Bird, who co-authored American Scoundrel with his wife Susan Goldmark, says Trump may have found his Cohn in Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation policies whom Trump just elevated to chief of staff. “It’s not really a surprise that, cornered and wounded by the recent election results, he reaches out and pulls up Stephen Miller, who’s very similar in his willingness to go on the offensive and never back down, and to say outrageous things to try to change the narrative,” says Bird.

Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to disenfranchise Black voters in the South this election cycle and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, she says there was “massive turnout” that propelled Democrats to victory. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated billionaire Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson, becoming the first Black woman ever elected governor in the United States. Incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff also handily won his bid for reelection.

articles.title: "The Earth Shook Last Night": Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Becomes First Latina Governor in Texas
articles.description: Texas Democrats have shattered more than three decades of Republican dominance in the state, winning races for U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and even railroad commissioner. They are also poised to possibly take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2003. The Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa, who defeated him by nearly 700,000 votes. She will be Texas’s first Latina governor. And James Talarico will be the first Democrat to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since 1993. “We’re celebrating these wonderful candidates who won office, and we’re also starting to think about what it means to hold power,” says Mike Siegel, a city council member from Austin, Texas, who founded Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. “We need to start thinking very quickly about how we will protect public education, how we will stop data centers and the encroachment of AI on our society, how we will protect public schools, how we stop collaboration with ICE .”

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Becomes First Muslim Senator as Democrats Rout GOP Across the U.S. in Rebuke to Trump
articles.description: In a stunning repudiation of President Trump, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. Meanwhile, progressive Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican Congressmember Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat in Michigan with over 52% of the vote. El-Sayed campaigned on a platform of Medicare for All, tackling economic inequality and getting big money out of politics — as well as ending military aid to Israel. He is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. El-Sayed faced vitriolic, Islamaphobic attacks by top Republicans throughout the campaign. “Last night wasn’t just about Dr. Abdulrahman being a Muslim, winning and going to the United States Senate,” says Palestinian American organizer and author Linda Sarsour, who has been campaigning for El-Sayed. “It demonstrated that progressives can win in states like Michigan” and that “we can win on standing up for the human rights of the Palestinian people.”

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it. articles.description: The Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey and Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan will answer your questions on Cop31, the draft deal on fossil fuels, the fight over climate finance and what overshooting 1.5C means for the world. The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is in its final days, and negotiators are fighting over a first draft of the deal. It calls for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, and for tripling adaptation finance for poorer countries. But with the world heading past the 1.5C limit and countries deeply divided over finance, adaptation and the “just transition”, can Cop31 deliver anything that matters? Continue reading...

Nobody in her family served, but my paternal grandfather fought in the Pacific in the second world war, and she was always grateful to hear his stories, even the repeats. It’s one of the things she gave me that I held on to, even in my worst years. The anger I’ve carried about the unjust wars of my lifetime – Afghanistan, Iraq and now Iran – never targeted the people sent to fight them. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
articles.description: Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds. Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic . “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.” Continue reading...

articles.title: I got scammed on Instagram – and it led to a truly disgusting dinner | Zoe Williams
articles.description: Intrigued by an unusual recipe for spinach tacos, I followed the instructions, but was left with a soggy, inedible mess. It turns out there are a lot of made-up meals out there I can’t tell you when my Instagram algorithm changed, from – this is embarrassing, but what the hell – buff guys trying to exercise and being interrupted by a Staffordshire bull terrier who wants to help them exercise, to cooking videos, but it has. I now get endless food content, following the same format: a millennial has 20 minutes to make dinner for his or her beloved (it’s very gender neutral), and launches into some unlikely techniques. He might shove a load of chicken into a cake tin, sprinkle mismatched spices all over, bake it, then slice it, as if it were a cake. Or she might cook tagliatelle in a pan of milk and salmon. This is not how it’s done, I think, as I watch all the way to the end, and then am astonished to be fed yet more weird food content. Drawn with an almost zombified lack of free will, I got the yen to try it for myself. What would happen if you boiled a white cabbage whole, then roasted it in honey and miso? Well, I can tell you: the cabbage is very soft on the outside, and still uncooked on the inside, and this is why cooks, since time began, have been slicing a cabbage before they try to cook it. articles.description: Poh Si Teng’s powerful documentary follows three doctors from the US who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital This is the latest documentary about medics travelling to Palestine to treat civilian casualties; it’s a powerful, angry film, in a state of despair at the scale of suffering and devastation. A sliver of hope is the trio of doctors it profiles, individuals acting on their conscience. (The same can be said of director Poh Si Teng , who quit her job at ABC News and cashed in her savings to get the documentary off the ground.) It follows three American doctors who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025 – though one of the trio, Thaer Ahmad, an ER doctor of Palestinian heritage from Chicago, is refused entry the night before they enter Gaza. His colleagues, Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon, and Dr Mark Perlmutter, a Jewish-American orthopaedic surgeon, complete the mission. This is not the first time in Gaza for either of them. Before he leaves, Perlmutter packs antibiotics into a dozen or so little plastic bags dotted around his luggage; that way if he gets turned back at the border, he stands a chance of getting some of the life-saving medication through. Given the high death rate of medics in the war, he also gets a will drawn up before he goes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so
articles.description: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood ‘Spit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones. It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies , Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”. articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You could argue this show cheats by cutting out that medieval context of prayer and faith. It’s also a great way for the gallery to show off that it owns three of his greatest portraits. Yet the result makes you see the utterly strange way he collects his slightly miniaturised people like flies in amber. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it
articles.description: As Sylvester Stallone’s Oscar-winning drama celebrates its 50th anniversary, I Play Rocky helps to further turn the boxing hero into the stuff of legend The story behind the making of Rocky has always sounded uncannily like Rocky itself. An unknown with an improbable dream, a skeptical establishment and a refusal to accept the odds: Sylvester Stallone’s real-life struggle to crack the industry and bring his breakthrough film to the screen contained all the elements of the underdog story he sought to tell. Now, half a century later, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky has crafted those parallels into a crowd-pleasing yarn of its own. It’s an extraordinary afterlife for a modest boxing flick that became the highest-grossing film of 1976 on a $1m budget and won the Oscar for best picture over one of the most stacked fields in history. Yet its greatest achievement may be the durability of the story – dismissed then by the New York Times as a “sentimental little slum movie” and Gene Siskel as a “flatout schmaltzy saga” – that we’re still finding new ways to repurpose all these years later through six Rocky films, three Creed sequels, a Broadway musical , and too many documentaries, novelizations and video games to count. At some point long ago, a screenplay written in three and a half days and never envisioned as IP became something closer to contemporary folklore. Continue reading...

articles.description: The Italian who became kingmaker in the world’s largest democracy charts her remarkable journey By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. articles.description: The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele. The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me ). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide , I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; most recently, an omnivorous Malaysian restaurant with a walloping double-tofu laksa, which shut 24 hours before publication. But the process encouraged me to take a different viewpoint, instead focusing on the spots that had survived and the story they told. articles.description: The wait for the new Bond is over but that’s only the beginning – there are still small issues such as the script, title, setting, casting, branding and promotion … • Robert Pattinson announced as James Bond – news • Share your thoughts on the casting • Peter Bradshaw’s take • Pattinson’s journey to James Bond • Behind Bond’s bankability It’s official: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond . While never a certainty for the role, for those reading the runes inside the film industry, the announcement will have been a tiny bit anticlimactic. Ever since it emerged that the film’s producers appeared unsatisfied with their initial shortlist and called in Pattinson alongside Nicholas Hoult, it appeared that in this new era for Bond under Amazon MGM, the traditional Bond barrier against an established Hollywood leading man was no longer in place. And with no shade to Hoult, Pattinson’s record at delivering in major franchises – Twilight, The Batman, Dune – as well as his classy acting CV put him firmly in the driving seat. In another departure from traditional 007 practice, Amazon MGM announced the casting decision via posts on social media , rather than at a press call in a fancy London hotel, which is how the world officially found out about George Lazenby, Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan . Although this will have been thought through as a way to maximise audience engagement with the forthcoming film, it perhaps is a disappointment to Bond purists that a big show wasn’t staged, and it may be Amazon MGM’s next order of business to organise a fan-type convention – or even piggyback on the next big fanclub event, due in December – to present Pattinson to an adoring audience. articles.title: Heysel 85 review – rage-filled denunciation of the incompetence that fuelled a football disaster
articles.description: Teodora Ana Mihai and her passionately committed cast reconstruct the grim sequence of bad judgments that led to 39 fans dying Shame and rage are the keynotes of this immersive, viscerally powerful drama-thriller set amid the macabre tragedy of football’s 1985 European Cup final between Juventus and Liverpool in the crumbling Heysel stadium in Brussels. Crowd disorder before kickoff in a poorly maintained, badly policed venue resulted in the deaths of 39 fans. In this film, the roar of the crowd echoing overhead through the stadium’s claustrophobic tunnels is like the wailing of the damned, while the sport’s officer class flinch and panic as if at a wartime loss. Grimly, the match was allowed to go ahead, despite the fatalities; the authorities believed the game itself would restore order on a bread-and-circuses basis, and that abandoning the match would only cause greater violence and chaos. Heysel 85 is directed and co-written by Romanian-born and Belgian-based film-maker Teodora Ana Mihai; she is a former collaborator of Cristian Mungiu, though maybe the influence here is more Paul Greengrass. The film-makers have been criticised for fictionalising aspects: the players are depicted as not being aware that fans had died before they took to the field – they were in fact largely aware, although it may well be true that the slippery authorities sought to minimise the truth as much as they could. And the fictionalised mayor of Brussels, here named Marc Dumont (Josse De Pauw), has been criticised as an unfair drunken caricature of the actual mayor, Hervé Brouhon. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
articles.description: Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place. Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its sequel, and we’re in metatextual heaven. In the four years of Westish time that have elapsed between the two books, Owen Dunne (baseball player in The Art of Fielding; groom-to-be here) has written and published, to great acclaim, a novel called – guess what! – The Art of Fielding. He riffled through her bags to choose a dress he told her she should wear for the date he’d be taking her on. And so began a short relationship – if that’s the right word, given she was still at school and he was a 30-year-old MTV presenter, who she says publicly referred to her as “the child”. Towards the end, she claims, Brand orally raped her . Lilly Creightmore was 18 when she says the then 32-year-old celebrity David Walliams asked her to dinner and then began pestering her for sex. articles.title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
articles.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily diaries, almost 100 notebooks, reels of letters, and four ledger books documenting Edward’s works. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
articles.description: It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing? In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate . In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble. Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m . Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Crimea bridge attacked again after Russia strikes major Kyiv bridges
articles.description: Ukraine again hits symbolic bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia; Kyiv’s heating and water disrupted as North and South bridges struck. What we know on day 1,728 Ukraine struck a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia for the second day in a row, after Moscow launched strikes on Kyiv’s bridges. Crimea’s Moscow-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces had struck the bridge and traffic had been suspended. On Monday, a Ukrainian drone crashed into one of the Kerch bridge’s arches . Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up. Russian strikes hit two major bridges in Kyiv late on Monday, part of an overnight attack that damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted heating and water in parts of the Ukrainian capital, its mayor said. The North and South bridges were hit, Vitali Klitschko said, citing preliminary information, in a post on Telegram just before midnight local time (2200 GMT), shortly after the Ukrainian air force warned of incoming missiles. He later said critical infrastructure systems were damaged and that heating and water supplies in some districts were affected. Air defence units were in operation in the city, he said, while witnesses ‌reported a series of loud explosions. Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier warned of an attack by Russia in the coming days . “Tonight, overnight and throughout tomorrow, please pay attention to missile danger alerts,” the Ukrainian president said in his nightly video address on Monday. “And they there, in Russia, must know that for every one of their evils there will be our just response.” Russia is receiving “dozens of missiles per month” from North Korea , Zelenskyy has said, citing

articles.description: Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech. “I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’” Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

articles.title: "We Have to Be Brave": Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Speaks Out After Israeli Detention
articles.description: The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara. “Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

articles.title: Pentagon Whistleblower Wes Bryant: Impeach Hegseth. He's a "Clear & Present Danger" to Democracy
articles.description: The House of Representatives is moving toward a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. They include violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. If the House votes for impeachment, it will prompt a Senate trial that could end with removal from office. “Under Hegseth, the U.S. military has been hijacked,” says retired Air Force Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, who served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to 2025. “America has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.” Bryant adds that “Hegseth should be the first domino,” but that Trump, as well as “many of our senior military leaders,” should also be impeached.

articles.title: Latino Voters Swing Away from Trump for "Terrorizing Our Communities": Marisa Franco of Mijente
articles.description: In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump. We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

articles.title: Election Protection: NAACP on Voter Suppression & Deployment of Federal Poll Monitors
articles.description: As President Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections, signaling his intentions to challenge results unfavorable to Republicans, we go to Washington, D.C., where a federal judge ruled Monday night that the Department of Justice can deploy election monitors to polling sites across the country, as long as they are not law enforcement officers with the power to make arrests. “In some respects, this is a victory for voters. Every voter in our country deserves to be able to cast a ballot today, free from intimidation,” says Kristen Clarke of the NAACP , which sued to challenge the DOJ’s plans to deploy ICE agents and other armed officers to the polls. The NAACP was also part of a coalition that intervened when the Trump administration attempted to force California to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleged were sent incorrectly to noncitizens. “This was a baseless, error-prone, shoddy 11th-hour attempt to hijack the election in California, plain and simple, and it’s now been rejected by four courts,” Clarke says. The administration’s attacks on voters “are not bearing fruit,” she adds. “We anticipate and are ready for anything that they may throw our way.”

articles.title: From Ranked-Choice Voting to Dumping Electoral College: Rob Richie on Election Reform Movement
articles.description: Alaska is the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of votes counted. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner. Rob Richie, president and founder of Expand Democracy and a senior adviser with FairVote, explains how ranked-choice voting has shaped the Alaska race and how it is “a system that promotes [candidates] reaching out, engaging, and, for voters, a lot of freedom.” Richie adds that Peltola is “heavily favored to win at this point.”

articles.title: Relatives of Slain Freedom Summer Activists Celebrate Scott Colom's Historic Senate Win in Mississippi
articles.description: Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The electoral breakthrough is particularly meaningful given Mississippi’s history in the civil rights movement. In 1964, three civil rights activists — James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman — were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan after traveling to the state to register Black voters. We speak with two of their relatives about Colom’s stunning upset. “I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed,” says Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney. “The people of Mississippi have spoken,” adds David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. “And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America.”

articles.title: Scott Colom Wins Stunning Victory, Becomes Mississippi's First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
articles.description: Democrat Scott Colom has made history as Mississippi’s first Democratic senator since 1982 — and its first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Colom’s victory brings the incoming Senate Democratic caucus to 55. Colom gave his victory speech on Wednesday at the historically Black Tougaloo College, just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan. “There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. articles.title: "They Have Eyes": How Trump's Corruption Became a Top Concern for Midterm Voters
articles.description: Democrats regained control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday’s historic midterm elections, a comeback fueled largely by voter anger over high prices and the war on Iran. But surveys also found that corruption was a major concern, with 76% of voters telling a Harris poll that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 63% of Americans considered it inappropriate for Trump and his family to profit from cryptocurrency, while 69% said his private business interests influence his decisions as president. “If this election was about corruption and cost, then this next Congress needs to be focused on accountability and affordability,” says Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW . “Congress needs to do oversight not just on the administration’s corruption, not just on the president’s profiteering, but also on corporate America, what they have gotten out of engaging in the president’s pay-to-play environment, how corporate America and the outside influence of money in our political system has undermined the public voice in our policy discussions.”

articles.title: First Gen Z Congresswoman: DSA's Melat Kiros on Corruption, Medicare for All & Israel
articles.description: The Democratic Socialists of America made major gains in this year’s U.S. midterms, electing not just the largest-ever socialist bloc to Congress, but also winning dozens of races at the state, county and municipal levels. Democracy Now! spoke with Congressmember-elect Melat Kiros on election night following her victory in Denver, Colorado. She identified Medicare for All as her top priority and said progressives must lay the groundwork “so that in ’29, when we have the House, the Senate and the White House, we can sign it into law on day one.” Kiros is a 29-year-old Ethiopian immigrant and lawyer. In 2023, Kiros wrote an open letter about the danger of conflating antisemitism and criticism of Israel, for which she was fired by her law firm. She won a major upset in the Democratic primary earlier this year against longtime incumbent Congressmember Diana DeGette.

articles.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
articles.description: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch. Continue reading...

articles.description: Andreeva seals 7-5, 6-3 victory to earn world No 2 ranking Russian dominates tournament without losing a set Mirra Andreeva had put herself on the brink of securing another effortless, straightforward set in one of the biggest finals of her career when she momentarily balked. This time, she betrayed no negative emotions at all. articles.description: It was the game to show Thomas Tuchel where his rebooted England team had got to; surely the ultimate test in international football. Spain in Spain. A world champion team who, in Tuchel’s words, had “forgotten how to lose.” Before this Nations League tie, they had been beaten only once in 43 matches – on penalties against Portugal in the final of this competition last year. articles.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
articles.description: Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations Your article ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century. There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
articles.description: Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
articles.description: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other. articles.description: Ulster Hall, Belfast With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers ‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage. They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. articles.title: Spark review – Glyndebourne Youth Opera light up a terrific new show of monsters and magic
articles.description: Glyndebourne, Lewes Lucy Armstrong’s family opera transports audiences to a secret world above the rooftops. It explores themes of grief and loss with a lightness of touch, and is directed, designed and performed with panache. For decades now, Glyndebourne has been setting the bar for what a youth opera company can be. Its latest show is Spark, a new full-length opera directed by Fiona Dunn with music by Lucy Armstrong, exploring grownup themes of grief and loss. Spark is a story of a parallel world accessed via something unlikely, so there are shades of Narnia or Wonderland. Our heroine is Clara (shades of The Nutcracker), who has panic attacks when she tries to go to school: “They talk like it’s simple,” she says in Olivia Bell’s succinct, fluent libretto, “but my chest is tightening and I can’t breathe.” We find out that her anxiety stems from her grief for her brother, and that she can no longer connect with her parents, who are having connection problems of their own. But she can escape up the chimney to a rooftop land populated by Spark Monsters – who will help her regain her lost spark, pun intended. Continue reading...

What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. articles.description: People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated? I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies , on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”. Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). Yet we’re still unhealthier than our elders? Continue reading...

articles.description: Slow-cooked pork in a deliciously sweet-salty glaze is Vietnamese comfort food at its best Many moons ago, I attended a cookery class in Hanoi that revealed to me the glories of thịt kho tàu , a simple but unbelievably delicious dish of caramelised pork braised in sweet coconut water and savoury fish sauce, enlivened by plenty of black pepper. In fact, loved it so much that I put their version in my cookbook, The A to Z of Eating, and then somehow forgot all about it for a decade. It’s easy to do that when you’re always working on the next recipe, but this week has been a very welcome rediscovery, not least because I’ve learned a lot more about what chef Thuy Diem Pham describes in her book The Little Viet Kitchen as “the ultimate home comfort food”. A family favourite, it’s also traditionally served as part of the lunar new year celebrations, because, in the words of Andrea Nguyen , “Tet is for savouring abundance, which explains why this rich, savoury braise of pork and eggs in bittersweet caramel sauce is a must-have”; and also, according to blogger Hungry Huy , “because of how well it keeps after cooking”. articles.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
articles.description: From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out? In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most. The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line , in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
articles.description: Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.” In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn , announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social homes target of 60%. But this was leavened with another bit of old-time Labour religion : “Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again.” John Harris is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
articles.description: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”. Continue reading...

articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

She and her costar Patricia Clarkson had graced the cover of Variety and appeared on The Kelly Clarkson Show. She had landed a part in NBC’s Quantum Leap revival. Then everything came crashing down. “I thought for sure I would have gotten some offers for a series regular on a TV show, which would have helped me finally buy a house,” recalls Lysette, who is trans. “But it didn’t come.” Instead, the calls stopped. articles.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
articles.description: In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage . When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan. Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Blacklock, Birmingham B3: ‘A very, very cool version of an Angus Steakhouse’ – restaurant review
articles.description: Ever-open, eminently relatable, sensibly priced spots of this sort will always have an audience A London chophouse has taken up residence on St Philip’s Place, Birmingham, on the edge of Cathedral Square, or “Pigeon Park”, as the locals call it. This particular nook of Brum city centre is a magnet to those feathered blighters, although Blacklock ’s smoulderingly macho menu is ironically pigeon-meat free, revolving instead around heaps of chops and steaks cooked over charcoal. There’s porterhouse, bone-in sirloin, lamb rump and pig’s head on toast. Launched in London in 2015 , Blacklock was the elegant, edgy, no-nonsense dining experience for groovy young things who quite literally wanted meat and two veg, so long as said veg was dripping-fat chips; it now has five sites in the capital and another in Manchester. “We just ended up at Blacklock,” people used to tell me half a dozen times a week, then go on to rave about the bread, the gravy and the ash-baked sweet potatoes, and revel in the glorious simplicity of it all. Modern life was complex, Blacklock was not, but neither was it cheap enough to feel like a jaunt down the Toby Carvery . And now its big flavours and broad appeal have hit the UK’s second city. articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. articles.title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
articles.description: As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us . Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé . We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience. A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may. My friends, it should be noted, felt the same. Thank God the heroic woman forced to endure Brand’s attack knew better. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Honey review – a hugely entertaining Killing Eve prequel that’s packed with naughty jokes
articles.description: This tale of a young female spy in 1980s East Berlin is a visual delight. Around every corner is a fun comic twist Is there any more alluring aesthetic in screen fiction than the iron curtain thriller? Any TV show dealing in 1980s cold war chic – Deutschland 83, Kleo, Star City, The Same Sky, the Russian bits of The Americans – probably has an irresistible mix of danger, absurdity and exotic kitsch. Moustaches! Wigs! Leather trench coats! Rigid patterned fabrics! Cassette players! Boxy cars! The chilly ennui of oppressed citizens and the flagrant risk-taking of secret agents, all somehow liberated by an existential inner emptiness! It’s just so much fun. Honey pitches us straight into premium frosty paranoia with an opening scene in which British “press attache” – ie spy handler – Graham Anderson (Rory Kinnear, hoorah!) endures a nervous crossing back into East Berlin, during which he really, really does not want his car to be searched. The crowning indignity of his interaction with a chortling buffoon of a border guard is when the manchild in uniform eyeballs Graham’s wife, Anne (Sonita Henry – a slightly more niche hoorah if you saw her fine turns in Silo or The Chelsea Detective), in the passenger seat and decides to show off how closely the pair are being surveilled: “Good luck for your smear test on Thursday, Mrs Anderson!” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘All I could smell was fertiliser’: the best (and worst) supermarket instant coffee, tasted and rated
articles.description: Our coffee snob spills the beans on which granules hint at chocolate and caramel, and which leave a bitter note • Everything you need to make great coffee I’m a coffee snob with my own grinder, but I found the haptic thwack, whack and crack of opening the lid and film on a jar of instant coffee strangely invigorating, and rather nostalgic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes of chicory, bitter chocolate and burnt sugar. Almost all of these products have a similar industrial imprint, uniform granules and a one-dimensional flavour profile, so they’re ultimately more a simulation of the real thing. That said, some did surprise me. At best, they taste like a cup of office filter coffee, made in a commercial drip machine and left just long enough for its aromas to fade. At worst, instant coffee tastes like cardboard and burnt rubber steeped in water. The addition of milk, however, transforms many cups and makes them far more drinkable and even comforting, bringing out notes of chocolate, nuts and caramel. Continue reading...

In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time. Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. articles.description: A historic single-track train line through the foothills of the Pyrenees opens up a pristine wilderness of forests, gorges and thundering rivers Alighting at the train station of Santa Linya in northern Spain, I paused to wonder what the railway engineers were thinking. A rough halt hewn out of the mountainside, with no ticket office, no waiting room, no sign of human habitation – just a single platform in the wilderness. On the far side of the track, a shimmering turquoise lake flanked by pine forests. Ahead – the only way out – a rocky trail snaking up the limestone cliff. My husband and I had first strayed into this western corner of Catalonia – Pallars Jussà – on our honeymoon road trip 21 years earlier. Seduced by its dramatic landscape of canyons, lakes, crumbling ruins and the formidable Noguera Pallaresa river thundering south from the Pyrenees, we had vowed to return one day. He loves mountains, I love water, we both love abandoned buildings; it was a geographical match made in heaven. Now those vows had come good – we were back, on a mission to go deeper into the hinterland. Continue reading...

articles.description: All of Hollywood’s biggest stars are in attendance for the Governors’ awards, but nobody gets drunk and the biggest draw is an awkward documentarian Timothée Chalamet was seconds away from getting into trouble. It was just after 6pm in Hollywood and Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was trying to corral a crowd of 700-odd people into sitting down so she could begin the Governors awards ceremony. She jokingly threatened to start calling out anyone still standing by name if they didn’t sit down imminently. Chalamet was the only one left on his feet, circling the table where he was due to sit next to his girlfriend, Kylie Jenner, opposite Tom Holland and Zendaya. Howell Taylor gave him a few seconds’ grace. He looked like the popular kid testing how far he could push a headteacher. The Governors awards had a curiously school-like atmosphere this year. Even the carpet in the Ray Dolby Ballroom was faded and striped. The social structure was much the same: closed-off and insular, with cliques, alliances, legendary enmities and intricate hierarchies of popularity and influence. There were those who seemed entirely comfortable – Chalamet, Holland, Tom Cruise, Matt Damon, Willem Dafoe, Seth Rogen – and others still angling for a better table. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
articles.description: Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to avoid pre-empting the broader “conversation” that he desires on relations with the EU. articles.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
articles.description: From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “ war minus the shooting ”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday? Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart the domestic rugby set-up in Wales; and the growing appeal of football . Until Saturday, Welsh sports fans looking for a winning finish were better off watching the darts champion Gerwyn “The Iceman” Price than Steve Tandy’s rugby team . The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. articles.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old. There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service , careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation , scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold , the leisure centres closed , the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back . That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech | John Crace
articles.description: The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser. For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never be wrong. Except when they are. The Guardian’s year in review 2026 .
