articles.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
articles.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams
articles.description: The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspective There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing. There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking about their parents. There are refugees en masse, shorn of any traits or qualities at all, discussed purely in terms of whether or not the host state can accommodate them, and how long they should be allowed to stay in any given place. articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
articles.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Though Trump is giving him the cold shoulder, Netanyahu is pulling out all the stops to cling to power. And he just might | Simon Tisdall
articles.description: The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet h is final downfall remains far from certain. As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary lengths to cling to power, using every dirty trick in his well-thumbed handbook while calling for a “government of national unity” (excluding Arab parties). And the perception he has been hung out to dry by a similarly electorally humbled Donald Trump , his biggest ally, may also prove over-optimistic. Besieged Palestinians in the West Bank and in hungry, flooded Gaza, and the bombed and battered people of Iran, have good reason to be fearful. articles.title: Filipiñana review – sexual exploitation at the golf club in menacing satire on class and privilege
articles.description: A sense of threat permeates a verdant private golf course in water-deprived Manila, peopled with submissive tee-girls and geisha-style caddies catering to the male clientele A spectacle filled with dreamlike tableaux, off-centre framing and slow trance-like zooms, Filipiñana is an elegant and politically pointed feature debut from the Filipino director and London Film School graduate Rafael Manuel, developed from his award-winning short film of the same name. It is a melancholy satire on caste shame, sexual politics and land exploitation in the Philippines, symbolised by a private golf course in Manila, an artificial landscape as depthless and surreal as the gardens in Last Year in Marienbad . Irrigating the vivid greens and undulating fairways requires oceans of precious water – water that, in the course of one unbearable heatwave, is rationed for the sweating lower orders in the city, way beyond the golf club’s luxurious precincts. Jorrybell Agoto plays the “Filipiñana” of the title, 17-year-old Isabel, the inscrutable witness to the club’s occult traditions and one of its legion of demurely submissive uniformed “tee-girls”, whose sole purpose is to position the balls for the wealthy (male) golfers about to tee off. (This is a task subject to much giggling innuendo in private among the girls themselves.) The tee-girls are not allowed to step on the course itself; that is the prerogative of the caddies, all women, each quaintly dressed in uniforms like that of an airline flight attendant, accessorised with a salakot -style peasant hat. articles.title: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey
articles.description: Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost . The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died. Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community alive. No – she was prophesying 40 years into the future about the digital-age phenomenon of ghosting. The fact that this practice is widespread enough for there to be a word for it is proof of the long since disintegrated fabric of our society. Temi Wilkey is a writer, performer and star of the one-woman shows Main Character Energy and Lover Girl , which is at the Soho theatre, London from 2 to 21 November Continue reading...

He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14. So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. articles.description: I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mr Baxter, who ate our belongings – and broke our hearts
articles.description: Reared on a puppy farm, and abandoned by a previous owner, he was half-starved when we adopted him. But he grew strong, chomping through everything from dog beds to sunglasses and my debut book The day we brought our 14-week-old cocker spaniel home in 2022, I was wearing a silk scarf I’d picked up decades ago in a vintage shop in Tokyo. I didn’t know it then but that rainy afternoon would be the last time I’d wear it. Three days later, it was in my new puppy’s mouth. Once he’d finished tearing my scarf to shreds, he gazed at me with soulful chocolate brown eyes, fluttering his long eyelashes. No matter how fond I was of that silk scarf, how could I be angry? Puppies chew stuff. That’s what they do. Mr Baxter gnawed his way through four dog beds, blankets and multiple dog leads. Nothing was off-limits. Socks, shoes, trainers, gloves, flat caps, berets, the freshly printed chapters of my debut book, a nifty pair of 70s sunglasses. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank. Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Already not at ease among his mates, Kate gets a ribbing when she repeats her UFO story (or Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, as they are called these days). And there are knowing glances about her psychiatric history: she once fended off an abusive boyfriend at knifepoint, insisting he was possessed. But if she is delusional, then it seems to be spreading: her one ally, spacey teacher Shelly (Ayvianna Snow), re-enters the room after a suspiciously long fag break, marvelling about how they will all imminently join “the light”. articles.title: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
articles.description: The latest in our series of writers picking their most comforting rewatches is a tribute to Curtis Hanson’s insightful 2000 comedy drama I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all. I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Even the misadventures of the film’s professor, Grady Tripp (Michael Douglas, never better), seemed romantic to me. On the eve of his university’s annual literary festival, Grady’s wife leaves him. His lover, Sara, announces she’s pregnant with his child. And James Leer, his brilliant but troubled student, who can rattle off Hollywood suicides in alphabetical order, shows up at the festival’s kick-off party cradling what may or may not be a cap gun. Grady responds to all this with the urgency of a veteran pot smoker – which he is. Continue reading...

articles.description: Theatr Brycheiniog, Brecon Puccini’s short comic opera comes to life with Richard Studer’s touring production, which leans into its commedia dell-arte elements In Dante’s Inferno, Gianni Schicchi de’ Cavalcanti, a 13th-century Florentine knight, was consigned to the eighth circle of hell for having been an arch-impostor. Puccini’s Gianni Schicchi, however, gets away with his blatant fraud, impersonating the newly deceased Buoso Donati and cheating his greedy relatives out of a large part of their rich uncle’s inheritance – albeit that they plotted with him to overturn the original will – to bag the best for himself. In this last of the Il Trittico triptych, Puccini allowed himself a lot of fun, and that too was the main ingredient in Mid Wales Opera’s SmallStages touring production. Tightly choreographed, with comedic energy and over-the-top characterisations, the commedia dell’arte element here bordered on farce, not least as the lugubrious crocodile tears of the shameless relatives waving their Pavarotti handkerchiefs gave way to boisterous remonstrations on learning that the whole estate had been left to a monastery. articles.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
articles.description: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones. articles.title: "Coffers Are Never Empty…For Bombs": Climate Activist Asad Rehman on Need for Climate Finance
articles.description: The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need. “Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, 'Our coffers are empty.' But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

articles.description: As delegates, industry lobbyists and civil society activists attend this year’s United Nations climate summit, known as COP31, we speak with international environmental lawyer Farhana Yamin about the state of global climate efforts. Yamin helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement and has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits. The Paris Agreement aimed to keep global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a threshold that climate scientists say the world will now overshoot. “It’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier,” says Yamin. “So, we’re about 10 years behind, but I hope that over time that we can accelerate.”

People, old and young, migrant and citizen, eat meals together made from food that would otherwise go to waste. The children play with donated toys, the grownups learn English together. articles.title: Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost album review – Anna Lapwood journeys to middle earth
articles.description: Lapwood/Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir (Sony) Lapwood has turned Howard Shore’s film score into an impressive full-blown organ symphony When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive. But wait, there’s more. Reckoning the symphony would benefit from the human voice, she incorporated a handful of songs, performing them live – in Tolkien’s Elvish dialect – while playing the Nidaros Cathedral organ in Trondheim, Norway. The results are frequently convincing, though the folksy music of the Shire is less effective on the organ than the baleful music of Sauron and the Ringwraiths. The latter in particular captures the sounds we associate with Widor, Boëllmann and Vierne in full gothic overdrive. If anything, Lapwood could afford to let rip more often, though her finger- and foot-work shine, as do the ethereal voices of the Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ma Wee Tin O’Shortbreid: a journey in search of the real Highlands
articles.description: Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became the title Growing up in Scotland, our family was one of many who kept their photographs in an old shortbread tin. The lid usually showed a castle beside a loch, a stag, a Highland coo and plenty of tartan. It was always sunny. Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid is Scots for “my little tin of shortbread”. The title started as a warning to myself: don’t make the Highlands look like a tin of shortbread. Isle of Mull. Out of the camper van, looking for white-tailed eagles. They were shot to extinction in Britain, the last one in Shetland in 1918. Brought back from Norway in the 1970s. Now they are one of the island’s biggest draws. A bird once shot on sight is part of the sales pitch. The Scotland on the lid promises wilderness and wildlife. The real one comes with binoculars and a long wait. Continue reading...

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Continue reading...

articles.title: Accidents, emotional affairs and impromptu Leonard Cohen dancing - My Wife Cries review
articles.description: Angela Schanelec’s famously uncompromising work takes on a new warmth in this sometimes playful study of everyday emotional turmoil The elliptical cinema of German film-maker Angela Schanelec is often described as uncompromising. This latest work, however, radiates a striking warmth. We see a marriage tearing at the seams, but this untethering is devoid of the usual dramatic flourishes. On an ordinary day like any another, construction worker Thomas (Vladimir Vulevic) notices a missed call from his wife, Carla (Agathe Bonitzer); when he phones back, she doesn’t pick up. The event holds little significance for the mild-mannered man; he carries on his usual chitchat with his co-workers, mundane catchups that unfold over static, tableaux-like shots. This deceptive calm is ruptured, however, when Thomas finds Carla sobbing helplessly on a park bench. A seismic change has taken hold within her: she will later confide in him of an emotional affair, and a tragic accident that leaves her emotionally unmoored. These revelations surface not through screaming matches, but by way of protracted conversations that resemble monologues rather than actual dialogue. Similar sequences recur as we are introduced to the rest of the couple’s social orbit, each of whom are wrestling with their own internal changes. There’s an enigmatic blend of theatricality and cinematic wizardry here; these wordy contemplations often occur when characters are on the move, walking, cycling or simply wandering about. There’s a subtle physicality and tactility to their inner struggles. Continue reading...

articles.description: From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants. And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care. articles.title: ‘A songbook for protest movements’: how did this secret mission to smuggle antifascist music out of Spain ever get forgotten?
articles.description: In 1961, a group of Italian creatives crossed the border to collect anti-Franco resistance songs and share them with the world – sparking intense backlash from the dictator. A new documentary retraces that perilous journey In the summer of 1961, four Italians crossed the Pyrenees into fascist Spain. Unknown to the border guards, their car was loaded with microfilm, a tape recorder and, tucked in the pocket of a writer and musician named Sergio Liberovici, a book of matches – each split in half, etched with the addresses of Spanish antifascists in miniature and glued back together, a hairline fracture concealing secrets that, if discovered, could result in jail or worse. Along with Michele Luciano Straniero, Emilio Jona and Margherita Galante Garrone, Liberovici was a member of a leftwing collective named Cantacronache. Formed in 1958 and counting Italo Calvino and Umberto Eco among their collaborators, the collective was repulsed by the superficiality of Italian pop music and hoped to revitalise culture with Brechtian realism. At the time, Italy was fiercely divided into leftwing and rightwing political camps, and it was a record label, Italia Canta, linked to the Italian Communist party, that financed the trip. articles.description: She has a rare debilitating skin condition but still tackled a marathon, helped by her old friend. As new film The Slightest Touch tells the full story of that emotional day, its stars talk about their lifelong bond – and why he opened up about parenthood Last month, HBO sent a private jet to Dublin to fly the star of a new documentary to London for the premiere. Colin Farrell appears in the film. But the private jet was not for him. The VIP passenger was Emma Fogarty, who has a rare, incurable genetic skin condition, epidermolysis bullosa or EB. Taking a commercial flight would have been physically impossible for her. As a publicist working on the film whispered to me, it was the one time you can emit all that carbon with a clean conscience. Fogarty was born 42 years ago. When she was diagnosed with EB, her parents were told she was unlikely to survive a week – which was probably for the best, said the doctor. With EB, the proteins that hold the layers of skin together are missing or faulty, leaving it as fragile as a butterfly’s wings. The slightest knock or bang can cause the skin to tear or blister; 80% of Fogarty’s body is without skin, and is wrapped in bandages to protect the wounds. Continue reading...

His usually bustling establishment – open from midnight to 7am – is empty. No one, he notes, will come: Covid-19 keeps them at home. An ironic start for a drama arriving after a seven-year absence, delayed in part by uncertainty over the pandemic’s impact on small eateries. The show’s return isn’t a shock. articles.title: "A Crackdown on All Independent Voices": Egypt Shutters News Outlets, Prosecutes Editor Lina Attalah
articles.description: Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , faces a criminal trial this week on charges of “spreading false information,” just two weeks after being convicted of operating an unlicensed website and fined more than $50,000. A judge also ordered the publication to be shut down. The cases are part of a broader crackdown on independent Egyptian media under the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, including the arrest of the entire newsroom of another outlet, Matsadaash . More than 100 organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and prosecutions and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges. “Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems,” Attalah told Democracy Now! in an interview Friday. “We need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms.” Attalah says she and Mada Masr will appeal the ruling to shut them down, hoping to “use this crisis” as a way to fight censorship in Egypt and expand the space for independent reporting.

articles.title: Simon Winchester obituary
articles.description: Intrepid writer and journalist who reported on the Troubles and Watergate, and whose string of bestsellers began with The Surgeon of Crowthorne The author and journalist Simon Winchester, who has died after a heart attack aged 82, thought himself lucky to have enjoyed “a pretty interesting, world-wandering life”. Those wanderings yielded a harvest of 30 books across a vast spectrum of subjects: from the land beneath to the wind above; from earthquakes to dictionaries, oceans to engines. The globe-trotting polymath, an American citizen from 2011, loved to take an everyday “invisible thing” in culture or nature – such as the winds of his final book, The Breath of the Gods (2025) – and show how it shapes private and public histories. We first knew about the Chornobyl disaster, which hastened the end of the USSR and a new geopolitical order, because an aberrant wind allowed Swedish scientists to measure the radioactive fallout freakishly blowing from Ukraine. articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
articles.description: Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations. After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas. Israel has repeatedly bombed medical facilities in Gaza since the start of the genocide in October 2023, even though such attacks are prohibited under international law. “It’s just barbarism. I don’t know why we’re supporting this,” says Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, one of the titular American doctors in the documentary, who demands accountability for Israel’s actions and a change in U.S. policy toward the country. “That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel.” Sidhwa also comments on the catastrophic flooding in Gaza that has swamped the temporary shelters of tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians as Israel continues to block the entry of shelter materials into the territory. articles.title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
articles.description: (Erased Tapes) Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr , in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir. On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. The resulting atmosphere sits somewhere between PJ Harvey’s late-90s eerie grunge and the trip-hop qawwali of Massive Attack’s work with singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan – an ambience that is as unsettlingly gloomy as it is engaging. Continue reading...

articles.title: "Parasitic Technology": Could Jensen Huang/Nvidia Scandal Prompt Rethink About AI?
articles.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries. Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk. We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA , who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

articles.title: Purple Mississippi? Overcoming GOP Voter Suppression, Black Voters Power Dem Wins Across the South
articles.description: Mississippi’s race for the U.S. Senate remains too close to call: Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,000 votes with 96% of votes counted as of Friday morning. Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 points in 2024. If elected, Colom would be the first Democrat to win the state in 40 years and the first African American since 1875, during the Reconstruction era. Colom, the former district attorney for northeast Mississippi, made the issue of affordability central to his campaign. He has sharply criticized national Democrats for writing off Mississippi and failing to invest in his campaign early on. “The entire country shifted left. But when you look at it regionally, the biggest shifts took place in the South — Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Louisiana,” says Cliff Albright, executive director of Black Voters Matter. That “wave of energy” was “largely led by Black voters who were most under attack with the mid-decade racial gerrymandering that was taking place. It clearly backfired, and all it did was to wake up a sleeping giant.” “Without the extreme gerrymandering, without the extreme voter restrictions that have been seen throughout the South, [the] wave would have been even bigger,” adds Chris Kromm, executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies. “There’s a real opportunity for engaging more voters and really pushing the region in a more progressive direction.”
